clue.text: Paint one in stripes ?

parts.note: read as two pieces, a word for paint followed by a description of a soldier wearing three stripes and a crown on his sleeve

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to decorate a person or object with painted stripes.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue splits into 'Paint' (COLOUR) and 'one in stripes' (SERGEANT, whose rank badge is chevrons), and together they name a senior army non-commissioned rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A colour sergeant is a senior NCO rank in British infantry and the Royal Marines, worn as stripes on the sleeve.

clue.text: Capital shape one's in after a nasty knock

definitions.text: Capital shape one's in after a nasty knock

parts.words: Capital shape one's in after a nasty knock
parts.note: capital means worn on the head, and the idiom 'knocked into a three-cornered hat' describes a thorough beating

explanation.surface: After a heavy blow, someone ends up in a fine state or shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' is not a city or money: it means of the head, so a 'capital shape' is headgear. To be knocked into a cocked hat is to be utterly defeated.
explanation.definitionFit: A cocked hat is a three-cornered headpiece, and the idiom about being knocked into one means thoroughly beaten.

clue.text: Cope with the wash, there below, on both sides of the Channel

parts.note: là is the French word for there, the Channel's far side
under means below, in English, this side of the Channel

explanation.surface: Doing the laundry is described as a chore on both sides of the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on both sides of the Channel' tells you one piece is French (là, there) and the other English (under, below).
explanation.definitionFit: To launder is to wash and iron clothes, which is coping with the washing.

clue.text: Experts in good form ?

parts.note: a school form or class containing the best pupils, and people who are experts in good manners or social form

explanation.surface: The question is who are the experts at behaving properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' plays two ways: a school class, where the top pupils are the 'upper' set, and good form meaning correct social behaviour, which the upper class are supposed to master.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest social rank is traditionally credited with knowing correct manners and etiquette.

clue.text: See 1
Fast time for a goose ?

parts.note: a season of fasting in the church calendar, with the name of a bird, the ember goose, attached

explanation.surface: Someone asks when a goose might go hungry, or move quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speed but means fasting: Ember Days are quarterly fast days in the Christian year, and the ember goose is an old name for the great northern diver.
explanation.definitionFit: Ember Days are four groups of three days of fasting and prayer through the church year.

clue.text: A Philistine runs out of oil but gets home

indicators.note: running out of a supply means having none of it left, so its letters leave the giant's name

parts.note: Goliath, the giant David killed, was the Philistines' champion
the three letters of oil are taken out, found in the giant's name as O, L and I

explanation.surface: A Philistine has no oil left but still makes it back to his house.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing O, L and I from GOLIATH leaves the city he came from. The feed's apostrophe in "'oil" is not on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: Gath was a Philistine city, named in the Bible as Goliath's own birthplace.

clue.text: Hospital worker might learn to go without the doctor

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the rearranged letters surround the doctor
go here means to go wrong or change, telling the solver the letters of learn are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
MO, medical officer, is a standard abbreviation for a doctor

explanation.surface: A hospital worker might be trained to manage when no doctor is present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' has its old meaning of outside, not lacking; 'to go' signals the rearrangement, giving ALNER around the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: An almoner was a hospital social worker who looked after patients' welfare and finances.

clue.text: Just as tea connoisseurs do, apparently

indicators.note: apparent means plainly visible, so the letters are in view across the words

explanation.surface: This describes doing something exactly the way tea experts do.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'jusT AS TEa'; 'tea' belongs to the hiding place, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Experts in food and drink sample and judge flavour, which is what they do.

clue.text: God's patent

parts.note: a thing only the Creator holds the rights to make, recalling a poem's line that only God can make one

explanation.surface: Something that belongs exclusively to God as his invention.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue recalls Joyce Kilmer's poem 'Trees': 'Poems are made by fools like me, But only God can make a tree.'
explanation.definitionFit: Kilmer's poem claims only the Creator can produce one, as though the design were his patented invention.

clue.text: Creditor takes a superior back seat

parts.note: CR is the standard abbreviation for creditor in bookkeeping
upper means superior or higher in rank

explanation.surface: A lender accepts a lesser, rear position behind someone more senior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back seat' is literal: the crupper is the strap under a horse's tail, or the horse's rump, behind the saddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A crupper is a horse's rump, the seat at the back behind the saddle.

clue.text: Punt to the half-back, early

parts.note: to punt is to place a bet

indicators.note: back tells you the word for half is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: semi is a prefix meaning half

explanation.surface: In a football match, someone kicks the ball to a half-back early in play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-back' looks like a football position, but it splits into two words: 'back' turns the word for half round, giving IMES.
explanation.definitionFit: Betimes is an old word for in good time or early.

clue.text: This wine makes one go wrong in the Spanish horse-race

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for the

indicators.note: in places the word for going wrong inside the race

parts.note: the Derby is the famous flat race run at Epsom in England
to err is to go wrong

explanation.surface: Drinking this wine makes a punter blunder at a Spanish race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is the English classic flat race run at Epsom; 'makes one' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderberry wine is a country wine made from the fruit of the elder tree.

clue.text: Flanders mare

parts.note: Henry VIII's alleged insult for a royal bride from Cleves, near Flanders, whose looks disappointed him

explanation.surface: A horse bred in Flanders.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a horse: 'the Flanders mare' was what Henry VIII reputedly called his fourth wife, Anne of Cleves.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry VIII's fourth queen, from Cleves, was reportedly mocked by him as a mare from Flanders.

clue.text: I am imprisoned without ten cents for obstruction

parts.note: I'm is the contraction of I am

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the word for imprisoned goes round the coin

parts.note: pent, as in pent up, means shut in
a dime is the American coin worth ten cents

explanation.surface: Someone jailed for lacking ten cents complains of the hindrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' has its old meaning of outside, not lacking: the word for shut in wraps round the American coin.
explanation.definitionFit: An impediment is a hindrance or obstacle.

clue.text: Gold-rush obstacles

parts.note: barriers that runners clear while racing for a gold medal, or the frames a prospector might use

explanation.surface: Difficulties faced by miners in a gold rush.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'rush' for gold is an athlete's dash for the winning medal, and what stands in the way are the barriers of a track race.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurdles are the barriers jumped in a race, and figuratively any obstacle.

clue.text: Has dinner, oddly enough, in court

indicators.note: odd means strange, so the letters of these two words are arranged in a strange new order

explanation.surface: Someone, surprisingly, takes a meal inside a courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews in ancient Jerusalem.

clue.text: Rank of Newbolt's sea-kings

parts.note: Henry Newbolt's poem '... All' praises Drake, Blake and other naval heroes

explanation.surface: A question about the standing of the naval heroes in Newbolt's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Henry Newbolt's poem 'Admirals All' celebrates English naval commanders such as Drake and Nelson, the 'sea-kings'.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest naval rank, held by the commanders celebrated in Newbolt's poem.

clue.text: Subsequently a friend on the side

parts.note: later means subsequently
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Afterwards, someone acquires a friend who takes their part.
explanation.definitionFit: Laterally means sideways, to or from the side.

clue.text: One never-to be-forgotten example led to more than rockets at the time

definitions.text: One never-to be-forgotten example led to more than rockets at the time

parts.words: One never-to be-forgotten example led to more than rockets at the time
parts.note: the rhyme 'Remember, remember the fifth of November' names gunpowder plotting; in 1605 it led to executions, today only fireworks

explanation.surface: A famous event once brought more than fireworks in its day.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guy Fawkes rhyme asks us to remember 'gunpowder, treason and plot'. Bonfire Night is now marked with rockets, but in 1605 the plotters were hanged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was an attempt to betray the king by blowing up Parliament.

clue.text: Home of Pope Gregory's angels

parts.note: Pope Gregory, seeing fair-haired slave boys in Rome, said they were not Angles but angels

explanation.surface: A question about where a pope's angels dwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Told the boys were Angles, Gregory the Great reputedly replied 'Non Angli sed angeli', and later sent Augustine to convert their land.
explanation.definitionFit: The Angles of Gregory's pun came from the land later named after them.

clue.text: Handy means of optical illusion

parts.note: handy points to the phrase 'of hand', a conjuror's dexterous trick that fools the eye

explanation.surface: A convenient way of creating a visual trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handy' does not mean convenient: it points to the conjuror's skill 'of hand', which deceives the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight of hand is manual dexterity used by a magician to deceive onlookers.

clue.text: It's hell in the valley of Hinnom

definitions.meaning: a biblical name for the place of punishment of the damned
a valley outside Jerusalem where children were once sacrificed, whose Hebrew name gave the word

explanation.surface: A grim description of the valley of Hinnom.
explanation.definitionFit: Gehenna, from Hebrew Ge Hinnom, was a valley near Jerusalem and became a name for the underworld of torment.

clue.text: He officiated at a maritime wedding

definitions.text: He officiated at a maritime wedding

parts.words: He officiated at a maritime wedding
parts.note: the ruler of Venice each year cast a ring into the Adriatic to marry the city to the sea

explanation.surface: Someone presided over a ceremony at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Venetian Sposalizio del Mare, the city's ruler dropped a ring into the sea, wedding Venice to the Adriatic.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief magistrate of Venice performed the yearly ceremony marrying the city to the sea.

clue.text: Curtails weeds

definitions.meaning: cuts short, as a tail or wages are cut
coarse broad-leaved plants of the sorrel family

explanation.surface: Someone cuts back the garden weeds.
explanation.definitionFit: To dock is to cut short or reduce, and dock is also a common broad-leaved weed.

clue.text: Benevolent man whose coin is not for the fountain

definitions.text: Benevolent man whose coin is not for the fountain

parts.words: Benevolent man whose coin is not for the fountain
parts.note: someone tossing a coin into a fountain for luck, read instead as a kind person

explanation.surface: A kindly man keeps his money rather than tossing it into a fountain.
explanation.walkthrough: People throw coins in a wishing well; the kind man of the clue 'wishes well' in spirit and keeps his coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-wisher is someone who wishes another person good fortune.

clue.text: Foreigner loses his head ? That's right

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: an alien is a foreigner

explanation.surface: An outsider panics, and someone confirms it is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's right' sounds like agreement, but 'right' is the definition in its legal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A lien is a legal right to keep someone's property until a debt is paid.

clue.text: Late fare for ancient Greeks

parts.note: late means dead: the coin placed in a dead person's mouth to pay the ferryman Charon

explanation.surface: Food served late in the evening to the ancient Greeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means deceased and 'fare' is a payment, not food: Greeks buried their dead with a coin for Charon's ferry.
explanation.definitionFit: The obol was a small Greek coin put with the dead as payment for the crossing of the Styx.

clue.text: Music room

definitions.meaning: describing music for a small ensemble, as in a string quartet

explanation.surface: A room set aside for music.
explanation.definitionFit: Chamber music is written for small groups of players, and a chamber is also a room.

clue.text: "A pulse in the mind " (Brooke)

parts.note: a quotation from Rupert Brooke's sonnet 'The Soldier' with one word missing

explanation.surface: A line from Rupert Brooke with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Brooke's 'The Soldier' ends with the English heart as 'A pulse in the eternal mind, no less'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word from Brooke's line describes the everlasting mind of God.

clue.text: Glides on in an oblique way

definitions.text: Glides on in an oblique way

indicators.note: oblique means slanting or indirect, so the letters move off their straight course into a new order

explanation.surface: Something slides along at an angle.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer and also builds it: the letters of 'Glides on' are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidelong means directed to the side, slantwise rather than straight.

clue.text: Firm going down Lovers' Lane ?

parts.note: a couple who are courting regularly are said to be 'going' with this firm word

explanation.surface: A business firm drives along a lane popular with couples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' is an adjective, not a company: courting couples are said to be 'going steady'.
explanation.definitionFit: Steady means firm and stable, and going steady is dating one partner regularly.
